title: Past papers · Your final topics

questions.title: When game theory helps
questions.stemHtml: Which activity is game theory particularly useful for explaining?

options.html: Strategic behavior among firms in an oligopoly

questions.answerHtml: Game theory studies choices whose payoffs depend on other decision makers’ choices. Oligopoly firms must anticipate their rivals’ responses.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Advertising: identify dominance
questions.stemHtml:
Rows: Firm A. Columns: Firm B. Each cell lists (Firm A, Firm B) profits.

Firm A / Firm BAdvertiseDo not advertise
Advertise(7, 1)(5, 4)
Do not advertise(3, 2)(2, 0)

Profits are in millions of dollars.

Which statement fits the matrix?

options.html: Firm A always receives less profit than Firm B
Firm A has a dominant strategy to advertise
Firm B has a dominant strategy not to advertise
Both firms have a dominant strategy not to advertise
Neither firm has a dominant strategy

questions.answerHtml: Compare Firm A’s first payoff within each column: advertising gives 7 rather than 3, and 5 rather than 2. Advertising is strictly dominant for A. B’s best response changes with A’s choice, so B has no dominant strategy.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Anticipate rivals’ reactions
questions.stemHtml: Which characteristic is especially associated with oligopoly?
questions.answerHtml: With only a few important competitors, one firm’s action affects the others and their responses affect its own profit. This strategic interdependence is why payoff matrices and game theory are useful.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Positive spillovers and output
questions.stemHtml: A competitive industry is in long-run equilibrium. Consuming its product creates positive external benefits. How does private output compare with the socially optimal quantity?

options.html: Production is possible only if the government gives a subsidy
Production is possible only if the government imposes a corrective tax

questions.answerHtml: Private buyers consider their own benefits but do not pay for the benefits received by others. MSB exceeds marginal private benefit, so the uncorrected market produces too little relative to the social optimum. A suitable subsidy can encourage extra beneficial consumption.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: A tax with vertical demand
questions.stemHtml: The government imposes a per-unit tax on producers. Demand is perfectly inelastic. What happens to the buyer’s price and quantity sold in the standard competitive diagram?
questions.answerHtml: A vertical demand curve fixes quantity. The tax shifts supply upward and raises the price paid by buyers, while quantity remains unchanged. In this model buyers bear the whole tax; the usual deadweight-loss triangle from a quantity reduction has zero width.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.stemHtml:

questions.title: Interdependence and games
questions.stemHtml: Game theory is most useful for describing markets in which:
questions.answerHtml: Strategic interdependence means each firm’s payoff depends on its own action and its rivals’ actions. Identical products alone do not tell us whether strategic interaction is important.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: A condition for price customization
questions.stemHtml: Which condition is needed for a seller to discriminate in price between customer groups?

options.html: Customers can freely resell the product
All buyers have identical demand elasticities
The seller can separate buyers according to their demand elasticities
Every buyer knows every other buyer’s price

questions.answerHtml: The seller needs market power and a way to distinguish customers with different willingness to pay or demand sensitivity. Resale must be limited so low-price buyers cannot undo the price difference by reselling to high-price buyers. The listed necessary segmentation condition is C.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Pollution and the welfare-loss area
questions.stemHtml: Which combination describes the externality and deadweight loss in the unregulated market?
questions.answerHtml: MSC > MPC signals an external cost. Private equilibrium is Q₂ where demand meets MPC; social efficiency is Q₁ where MSB meets MSC. The lost surplus from excess output Q₁–Q₂ is the area egh between MSC and MSB, not the entire external-cost rectangle.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Choose the corrective tax
questions.stemHtml: Which policy can correct this externality in the graph?
questions.answerHtml: A corrective tax equals marginal external cost at the efficient output. Here the parallel MSC and MPC curves have constant vertical separation P₄ − P₂, also equal to P₃ − P₁. It shifts private marginal cost up to social marginal cost, reducing output to Q₁.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Tax and consumer surplus
questions.stemHtml: A per-unit tax is placed on personal computers in a standard competitive market. How does consumer surplus change?

options.html: It decreases because buyers pay a higher price
It decreases because more computers are supplied
It increases because firms pass the tax to consumers
It increases because consumers buy more imports
It is unchanged because demand is unit elastic

questions.answerHtml: The tax creates a wedge between the buyer’s price and the seller’s net price. Buyers pay more and buy fewer units, reducing the area of consumer surplus under demand and above their price.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Who bears more of the tax?
questions.stemHtml: Corn supply is relatively price inelastic and demand is relatively price elastic. Who bears more of a per-unit tax on corn production?

options.html: Buyers and sellers bear equal shares

questions.answerHtml: The less price-responsive side bears more of the tax. Suppliers cannot reduce quantity as easily as buyers can, so more of the wedge comes from a lower net price received by sellers. Who legally pays the tax does not determine its economic burden.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Why a cartel member cheats
questions.stemHtml: Four oligopoly firms coordinate to maximize combined industry profit. One firm secretly cuts its price or sells more than agreed. What is the short-run consequence assumed in this cartel question?

options.html: The cheating firm’s profit rises; total industry profit falls
Both the cheating firm’s profit and industry profit rise
Both the cheating firm’s profit and industry profit fall
The cheating firm’s profit falls; industry profit rises
The non-cheating firms earn higher profits

questions.answerHtml: The cartel jointly restricts output to maximize combined industry profit. A member can gain privately by undercutting or expanding while others honor the agreement, but this erodes the jointly optimal restriction. This incentive to defect helps explain the prisoner’s dilemma and why punishment in repeated interaction can matter.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Taxing an already underprovided good
questions.stemHtml: In a competitive market with ordinary upward-sloping supply and downward-sloping demand, MSB exceeds MSC at private equilibrium. What would a new per-unit production tax do?
questions.answerHtml: MSB > MSC means an additional unit creates a net social gain, so the market is already producing too little. A production tax reduces quantity further and widens the welfare loss. A policy’s effect depends on the direction of the original distortion.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: What dominance means
questions.stemHtml: In a two-firm market, what does it mean for one firm to have a dominant strategy?

options.html: It keeps that strategy whatever the competitor chooses
It changes strategy whenever the competitor changes
It moves first and waits for a response
It must collude to remove uncertainty

questions.answerHtml: A dominant strategy is a best choice against every action of the opponent. It does not mean moving first, and a firm can have a best response without having a dominant strategy.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Recognize a concentrated oligopoly
questions.stemHtml: The four largest firms produce 88% of industry output. Which market structure best fits?
questions.answerHtml: A small group of large sellers dominating output is characteristic of oligopoly. Concentration is a clue that strategic interaction may matter; it does not by itself prove a particular markup or monopoly power.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Tax wedge and lost surplus
questions.stemHtml: A $4 per-unit tax is imposed on sellers. Choose the buyer price, seller’s after-tax price, and deadweight loss.
questions.answerHtml: The $4 wedge fits between demand at $8 and supply at $4 at Q = 100. Before the tax, Q = 200. The lost-surplus triangle is ½ × (200 − 100) × 4 = $200. Tax revenue is a transfer to government and is not itself deadweight loss.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Newspapers: one dominant strategy
questions.stemHtml:
Rows: Daily Voice. Columns: Town Herald. Each cell lists (Daily Voice, Town Herald) profits.

Daily Voice / Town HeraldNo price changeIncrease price
No price change(500, 400)(200, 700)
Increase price(600, 300)(300, 100)

Which statement about dominant strategies is correct?

options.html: No change is dominant for Daily Voice
No change is dominant for Town Herald
Increasing price is dominant for Daily Voice
Increasing price is dominant for Town Herald
Neither firm has a dominant strategy

questions.answerHtml: Daily Voice compares its first payoffs by column: 600 > 500 and 300 > 200, so increasing price is dominant. Town Herald prefers an increase when Daily Voice holds price (700 > 400), but no change when Daily Voice raises price (300 > 100). It has no dominant strategy.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Perfect price discrimination
questions.stemHtml: What does a firm doing perfect price discrimination charge?

options.html: Each customer the highest price that customer is willing to pay
Each customer the lowest price that customer is willing to pay
Prices differentiated only by quantity purchased

questions.answerHtml: Perfect or first-degree price discrimination extracts each unit’s willingness to pay. In the standard model it transfers consumer surplus to the seller and expands sales toward the efficient quantity. Age discounts are group pricing, not perfect discrimination.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Why pollution creates overproduction
questions.stemHtml: Why is the efficient output below the private competitive output when production creates pollution?

options.html: Total social cost is below total social benefit

questions.answerHtml: Production imposes costs on outsiders, so MSC = MPC + marginal external cost. Private suppliers use MPC; society must count MSC. The efficient intersection MSB = MSC occurs at a lower quantity than the uncorrected private equilibrium.
questions.answerOrigin: Study explanation checked against the answer key included in the uploaded paper

questions.title: Perfect price discrimination
questions.stemHtml: Which statement is NOT true about a seller engaging in perfect price discrimination?

options.html: The monopolist needs to know each consumer’s maximum willingness to pay.
The monopolist’s profit is total surplus minus fixed costs.
Perfect price discrimination results in zero deadweight loss in the market.
Perfect price discrimination is allocatively inefficient.
The monopolist produces where demand intersects marginal cost.

questions.answerHtml: Under the ideal model, each buyer pays their willingness to pay and every unit with willingness to pay at least MC is sold. Output is allocatively efficient, consumer surplus is zero, and the output-related deadweight loss disappears. Thus the claim of allocative inefficiency is false. Fixed costs still matter for profit; there are no externalities or implementation costs in this model.
questions.answerOrigin: Study solution checked against the supplied key

questions.title: Read the external benefit
questions.stemHtml: The graph illustrates a market with which externality?

options.html: A positive externality in consumption of $14 per unit
A negative externality in consumption of $10 per unit
A positive externality in production of 100 units
A positive externality in production of $4 per unit
A negative externality in production of $10 per unit

questions.answerHtml: MSB lies above MPB, so consumption creates an external benefit. Compare the two benefits at the same quantity: 44 − 30 = $14 at Q = 400, or 34 − 20 = $14 at Q = 500. The 100-unit output gap is not a dollar measure of the marginal external benefit.
questions.answerOrigin: Study solution checked against the supplied key

questions.title: Guava externality: parts a–b
questions.stemHtml:
Bueno produces guava in a perfectly competitive market. Use the supplied graph.

  1. a. Identify the market failure.
  2. b. Use numbers from the graph to identify the marginal external benefit.

Only parts a–b are included. Parts c–d concern labor hiring and monopsony and are outside this focused set.
questions.answerHtml:
a. A positive consumption externality: MSB exceeds MPB, while MPC = MSC. The unregulated market produces Q0, below efficient output Q1.

b. Compare the two benefit curves at the same quantity. At Q0, external benefit = 8 − 5 = $3 per unit. At Q1, it is 7 − 4 = $3 as well. Do not subtract benefit at one quantity from benefit at another.
checks: Explained MSB > MPB and MPC = MSC.
Distinguished private output Q0 from efficient output Q1.
Calculated MEB = $3 using both curves at the same quantity.
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no official marking rubric supplied

questions.title: Move to perfect price discrimination
questions.stemHtml: A profit-maximizing seller begins perfect price discrimination. Which outcome follows under the paper’s standard model?
questions.answerHtml: Charging willingness to pay lets the seller capture surplus previously left to consumers and earn more profit than under a single price. Standard perfect discrimination expands output toward P = MC and reduces the output distortion. It does not lower the production cost curve.
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no answer key was included in the 2024 upload

questions.title: Which coffee market is an oligopoly?
questions.stemHtml: Which description best illustrates oligopoly?

options.html: CoffeeBar can sell any quantity at the market price but loses all customers if it charges more
CoffeeBar is the only coffee shop and earns positive long-run profit
CoffeeBar is the only employer of beverage-service workers
CoffeeBar is one of many differentiated coffee shops and earns zero long-run economic profit
CoffeeBar is one of two shops and repeatedly offers discounts to win customers from the other

questions.answerHtml: Two competing sellers making promotions in response to each other illustrate strategic interdependence. The other descriptions depict price taking, monopoly, monopsony, or monopolistic competition.
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no answer key was included in the 2024 upload

questions.title: Tax and producer surplus
questions.stemHtml: How does the per-unit tax change producer surplus?
questions.answerHtml: Before tax, producer surplus is ½ × 30 × $3 = $45. After tax, Q = 20, buyers pay $4, and sellers keep $2 after the $2 tax. Producer surplus is ½ × 20 × $2 = $20. The change is $20 − $45 = −$25. Use the seller’s net price, not the buyer’s price.
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no answer key was included in the 2024 upload

questions.title: Internalize a $20 external cost
questions.stemHtml:
The market is initially in private equilibrium. Each unit produces a constant external cost of $20. Which action improves efficiency?

QuantityMPC ($)MPB ($)
212565
223555
234545
245535
256525

options.html: Tax producers $20 per unit; output falls to 22
Tax consumers $20 per unit; output falls to 21
Subsidize consumers $20 per unit; output rises to 25
Subsidize producers $20 per unit; output falls to 21
Set a $20 price floor; output rises to 24

questions.answerHtml: Private equilibrium is Q = 23, where MPC = MPB = 45. With no benefit spillover, MSB = MPB. At Q = 22, MSC = MPC + external cost = 35 + 20 = 55, equal to MSB. A $20 producer tax makes the firm face the full marginal social cost and achieves Q = 22. A consumer tax of the same size could create the same wedge, but option B’s quantity 21 is wrong.
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no answer key was included in the 2024 upload

questions.title: Choose the size of a subsidy
questions.stemHtml: The government wants quantity to rise to 300 units. Which intervention achieves that target?

options.html: A $2 consumer subsidy plus a $2 producer tax
A $2 consumer subsidy plus a $2 producer subsidy

questions.answerHtml: At Q = 300, suppliers require $8 while buyers will pay $4. The needed subsidy wedge is $4 per unit. A $2 subsidy on each side supplies that total wedge. A single $2 subsidy is too small; an equal subsidy and tax cancel. Increasing quantity does not by itself prove a welfare improvement.
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no answer key was included in the 2024 upload

questions.title: Waste management: simultaneous choices
questions.stemHtml:
Rows: Bygone2. Columns: Cleared4U. Each cell lists (Bygone2, Cleared4U) profits.

Bygone2 / Cleared4URecyclingComposting
Recycling(45, 47)(42, 37)
Composting(38, 43)(40, 41)

Both firms have complete information and independently choose at the same time. Which statement is true?

options.html: Neither firm has a dominant strategy
Both have a dominant strategy to choose composting
Both have a dominant strategy to choose recycling
Cleared4U chooses recycling dominantly; Bygone2 chooses composting dominantly
Bygone2 chooses recycling dominantly; Cleared4U chooses composting dominantly

questions.answerHtml: Bygone2 compares first payoffs by column: recycling gives 45 > 38 and 42 > 40. Cleared4U compares second payoffs by row: recycling gives 47 > 37 and 43 > 41. Both have strictly dominant recycling strategies, giving the dominant-strategy outcome (45, 47).
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no answer key was included in the 2024 upload

questions.title: Subsidy without an externality
questions.stemHtml: In a standard competitive market with no externalities, the government increases a per-unit subsidy to consumers. Which outcome follows?
questions.answerHtml: A consumer subsidy shifts effective demand upward, increasing quantity and the price received by sellers, so producer surplus rises. The government spends money; it does not gain tax revenue. With an initially efficient competitive market, the subsidy pushes output beyond the efficient quantity and creates or increases deadweight loss.
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no answer key was included in the 2024 upload

questions.title: Match the tax to marginal damage
questions.stemHtml: Which listed policy corrects the externality?
questions.answerHtml: Efficient output is Q₁ where MSB = MSC. Marginal external cost at Q₁ is the vertical gap MSC − MPC = P₃ − P₁. A tax of that amount internalizes the external cost. Q₂ is already the excessive private output, so limiting production to Q₂ does not correct it.
questions.answerOrigin: Independent study solution; no answer key was included in the 2024 upload

questions.title: Price customization and substitutes
questions.stemHtml: A firm sells its product in two separate markets. If it practices price discrimination, it is most likely to charge a higher price in the market that
questions.answerHtml: Fewer close substitutes generally make demand less price elastic. Under the usual comparison with the same MC and effective market separation, the less elastic market supports a higher optimal price. Different marginal costs could change the comparison; resale can undermine discrimination.
questions.answerOrigin: Study solution checked against the handwritten answer in the supplied copy

questions.title: Advertising dominant strategies
questions.stemHtml:
Nick’s Barbecue and Frank’s Barbecue choose independently and simultaneously with complete information. The first entry is Nick’s payoff; the second is Frank’s. Which pair describes their dominant strategies?

Nick’s / Frank’sAdvertiseNot advertise
Advertise$600, $100$360, $250
Not advertise$370, $140$350, $150

options.html: Nick: Not advertise; Frank: Not advertise.
Nick: Advertise; Frank: no dominant strategy.

questions.answerHtml: Nick prefers advertising against either Frank action: 600 > 370 and 360 > 350. Frank prefers not advertising against either Nick action: 250 > 100 and 150 > 140. Thus the dominant-strategy outcome is (Advertise, Not advertise), with payoffs (360,250).
questions.answerOrigin: Study solution checked against the handwritten answer in the supplied copy

questions.title: Recognize a negative production externality
questions.stemHtml: Which is an example of a negative externality in production?

options.html: An electronics store cuts television prices during the holidays.
A car insurer charges teenage drivers a higher price.
A local paper mill emits an odor, imposing additional costs on nearby residents.
A pine tree in a public park provides pleasant shade for residents.
A photographer accepts a price below marginal cost.

questions.answerHtml: The paper mill’s production imposes a cost on neighbors outside the transaction. This can make MSC exceed MPC and lead to excessive production. A price change or a producer’s loss is not, by itself, evidence of an externality.
questions.answerOrigin: Study solution checked against the handwritten answer in the supplied copy

questions.title: Collusion and lost surplus
questions.stemHtml: The only two firms in an industry collude to charge a higher price and produce less than the socially optimal quantity. What happens to consumer surplus and total economic surplus in the short run?

options.html: Consumer surplus decreases; total surplus stays the same.
Consumer surplus decreases; total surplus increases.
Consumer surplus increases; total surplus decreases.

questions.answerHtml: Consumers lose surplus because of the higher price and fewer purchases. Some of that loss transfers to producers, but restricting beneficial trades creates deadweight loss, reducing total surplus. A transfer alone does not account for all of the consumer loss.
questions.answerOrigin: Study solution checked against the handwritten answer in the supplied copy

questions.title: Government spending on a subsidy
questions.stemHtml: The letters represent enclosed areas. What is the total cost of the per-unit producer subsidy to the government?

options.html: Areas A, B, C, F, G, H, and J
Areas A, B, C, D, F, J, and K

questions.answerHtml: The subsidy per unit is the seller receipt P1 minus the buyer price P3. Multiply this wedge by Q2. The resulting rectangle covers A + B + C + F + G + H + J. This is the government’s budget cost, not automatically the welfare loss. The source’s “Supply + Subsidy” label denotes the lower effective supply curve facing buyers.
questions.answerOrigin: Study solution checked against the handwritten answer in the supplied copy

questions.title: Consumer surplus after a subsidy
questions.stemHtml: The increase in consumer surplus caused by this producer subsidy equals
questions.answerHtml: Consumer surplus expands when the buyer price falls from P2 to P3 and purchases rise from Q1 to Q2. Relative to the original consumer-surplus triangle A, the added area is B + C + J. The subsidy budget rectangle is larger than this consumer gain.
questions.answerOrigin: Study solution checked against the handwritten answer in the supplied copy
